publisher_issuer: Wikipedia (aggregating CNET News, Reuters, and contemporaneous reporting)
company_context: Pets.com was a U.S. online pet-supplies retailer that IPO'd in February 2000 at $11 per share and announced its shutdown on November 7, 2000, ceasing orders November 9, 2000, only 268 days after going public. It became an emblematic dot-com bust.
evidence_summary: Pets.com sold products, notably heavy bagged pet food, below cost while offering free or heavily subsidized shipping, producing persistent negative gross margins. After the dot-com funding window closed, it could not raise more capital and liquidated within the year of its IPO. Reporting consistently frames the failure as a structural unit-economics problem (losing money on each sale) rather than a demand problem.
outcome_evidence: Company announced shutdown on November 7, 2000, ceased taking orders November 9, 2000, laid off 255 of 320 employees, stock fell from $11 IPO price to $0.19, and was liquidated (renamed IPET Holdings) by January 2001. Approximately $300 million of invested capital was lost.
source_limitations: Wikipedia is a tertiary aggregator; the underlying primary CNET/Reuters articles from 2000 could not be fetched directly in this environment (403/blocked). Figures here were confirmed verbatim across multiple credible WebSearch snippets, but the per-dollar loss figure (26 cents) is widely cited secondhand and should be treated as reported rather than audited.
directly_stated: Shutdown announced November 7, 2000; orders ceased November 9, 2000
Sold pet food below cost with subsidized shipping (negative gross margin)
inferred: The negative gross margin made scale actively harmful (more sales meant more losses)
Demand existed (orders were being placed) but could not be served profitably
why_useful_for_opsiq: Canonical unit_economics_failure where revenue growth masked a structurally unprofitable cost-to-serve. Tests whether a diagnostic system can distinguish a demand problem from a margin/cost-structure problem and avoid the trap of recommending 'grow faster' when each incremental sale destroys value.
